title: A comprehensive AMR genotype-phenotype database (CABBAGE).

verified.what_i_actually_checked: Downloaded and opened the 2026-07 release from the EBI FTP site: phenotype.parquet (1,714,486 rows, 34 columns, 170,750 BioSample IDs), genotype.parquet (1,370,205 AMRFinderPlus hits across 164,840 isolates) and the merged file (109,338 rows). The S/I/R (susceptible/intermediate/resistant) label is filled in 1,379,999 rows. Units: mg/L for 1,246,129 rows and mm for 34,424. Of the 1,372,970 isolate×drug pairs, 7,012 appear more than once and 4,662 conflict. 97% of phenotype rows have an isolate with genotype hits, and 240 species×drug combinations have at least 500 genotyped, labelled isolates. Collection years run from 1911 to 2025 (22% missing); 153 countries. Klebsiella meropenem check: 1,642 of 1,932 carbapenemase carriers are resistant, against 184 of 3,120 non-carriers. M. tuberculosis has 0 point-mutation calls.
verified.what_came_from_paper_text_only: The curation rules (how MIC values were cleaned, why the 9 source databases were chosen), the assignment of 'Updated_phenotype_CLSI/EUCAST' labels by re-applying clinical breakpoints, and the restricted ATLAS comparison set (on Vivli, by application) come from the paper only. I did not open the per-genome GFF/TSV files or portal.duckdb (174 MB).

a1_downloadable.note: Open parquet/CSV files on the EBI FTP site, no login; verified by download. Only the ATLAS comparison set needs an application, and it isn't needed here.

a2_label_is_a_column.note: 'resistance_phenotype' (S/I/R) and 'measurement' (MIC, the minimum inhibitory concentration, or zone diameter) are columns in phenotype.parquet. Nothing has to be constructed beyond pivoting the gene hits per isolate.

a3_inputs_present.note: Inputs are AMRFinderPlus resistance-gene and point-mutation calls per isolate, already in genotype.parquet and keyed on BioSample. Whole genomes are not included, and pulling them for every isolate would mean about 165k downloads.

a4_units_stated.note: There is a measurement_units column (mg/L or mm), and a measurement_sign column marks censored values such as <= or >. Verified in the file.

a5_enough_rows.note: 1.38M labelled isolate×drug rows; 240 species×drug pairs have 500 or more genotyped isolates. Verified.

a6_fits_laptop.working_set: ~40 MB parquet; a pivoted binary matrix of ~165k isolates × ~2,000 genes, stored sparse
a6_fits_laptop.note: The three main files total 41 MB; pandas loads them in seconds.

a7_counts_match_paper.note: The paper says over 170,000 isolates and about 1.7M pairs; the file has 170,750 BioSamples and 1,714,486 rows. They match.

a8_label_provenance.note: The label is a lab susceptibility test (broth/agar dilution, disk diffusion or E-test, a gradient-strip test). It is not a model output and is not computed from the gene calls. Caveat: BV-BRC (the bacterial bioinformatics database, formerly PATRIC) also hosts computer-predicted resistance; the curated table should hold lab tests only, but check the PATRIC rows for any 'computational' method.

B1.why: Two tables (phenotypes, gene hits) join cleanly on BioSample_ID; 97% of phenotype rows match. Verified.

B2.why: Parquet parsed first try with pyarrow; columns are typed.

B3.why: S/I/R labels mix CLSI and EUCAST guidelines (the US and European breakpoint standards) across years; re-standardised columns are only ~55% filled.

B4.why: About 47% of MICs are censored (<=, >, >=); the binary S/R label avoids most of this.

B5.why: 7,012 duplicated isolate×drug pairs, 4,662 of them conflicting, out of 1.37M; easy to drop.

B6.why: Fields are documented in the paper's tables and the portal docs; columns are self-explanatory in the file.

C1.why: 'Where do known-gene rules fail, by species, country and year?' is informative whichever way it comes out.

C2.why: Open models exist (Kover, ResFinder, amR, a 2024 benchmark), but they were trained on PATRIC subsets (31k genomes), not 165k isolates.

C3.why: Better/diversity angle: largest public table, 58 species and 153 countries, enabling country and time holdouts nobody has run at scale.

C4.why: Lab susceptibility testing takes days but is cheap; genome-based testing is the stated clinical goal.

C5.why: Obvious rule baseline (any known gene for the drug class means resistant) and majority-class dummy, both computable from the files.

D1.why: ESM-2 (a protein language model) could embed the ~2,177 reference proteins of the gene hits; useful, but a side feature.

D2.why: Embed ~2,177 proteins once on CPU, then fit a gradient-boosted or logistic head.

D3.why: EMBL-EBI data are open; ESM-2 is MIT-licensed; AMRFinderPlus is public domain.

E1.why: Hold out by country, source study (AMR_associated_publications) or collection year; columns verified.

E3.why: Majority class per species×drug, plus a known-gene rule baseline.

E4.why: 4,662 conflicting duplicate labels across sources give a measurable disagreement floor.

E5.why: Verified: Klebsiella carbapenemase carriers 85% meropenem-resistant vs 6% of non-carriers.

E6.why: Label shuffling and dropping the matching gene class are trivially runnable.

E7.why: A year column (78% filled) and a database-source column allow temporal and source holdouts.

E8.why: Published numbers (2024 benchmark, amR) use different PATRIC subsets or genome features; not directly reproducible from these calls.

G1.why: Standard IDs in the file: BioSample, assembly accession, NCBI taxon ID, ARO antibiotic ontology, RefSeq protein accessions.

G2.why: CARD (resistance gene database) or WHO's tuberculosis mutation catalogue are plausible partners; the join adds little beyond what's already there.

G3.why: Isolate to drug labels is cleanly one-to-many; gene hits pivot to a binary matrix.

G4.why: Adding protein embeddings asks whether unseen gene variants can be scored; only marginally bigger.

H1.why: Both outcomes present: 1.04M susceptible and 303k resistant rows, verified.

H2.why: 58 species, 153 countries, 64 source combinations; skewed to North America (43% of rows).

H3.why: Claim stated precisely below, including the known-gene-only and sequenced-isolate biases.

H4.why: Paper discusses mixed guidelines and the recent-year lag; the missing tuberculosis mutation calls are not flagged.

I1.why: The CABBAGE authors (Imperial MRC Centre, EMBL-EBI) and the AMRFinderPlus/ResFinder curators.

I2.why: Showing where gene catalogues miss resistance could focus catalogue curation.

I3.why: Sensitivity for resistance (calling a resistant bug susceptible is the costly error) is the clinical decision itself.

I4.why: Rules already work well, e.g. carbapenemases; ML is likely to help only for multi-gene and low-prevalence cases.

J1.why: Grouped splits, temporal holdout, rules-versus-ML comparison, optional protein embeddings.

J2.why: Textbook resistance mechanisms give sanity checks; clinical breakpoint nuance needs a microbiologist.

J3.why: Rule-failure map per species×drug is shareable before any model.

J4.why: Can be scoped to 3 weeks, but not yet written down.

J5.why: No kill date recorded in NOTES.md yet.

existing_models.name: 2024 benchmark of Kover, PhenotypeSeeker, Seq2Geno2Pheno, Aytan-Aktug and ResFinder (Briefings in Bioinformatics, bbae206)
existing_models.score_and_split: F1-macro (balanced accuracy-type score) ≥0.9 in 64% of experiments on random folds, falling to 25% on phylogeny- or homology-aware folds; 78 PATRIC datasets, 31,195 genomes, 11 species.
existing_models.authors_named_unsolved: Robust prediction for strains that diverge from the training set; rule-based ResFinder beat ML on divergent strains.

existing_models.name: amR (JRaviLab, an R package suite)
existing_models.score_and_split: Median MCC (Matthews correlation coefficient, a balanced score from -1 to 1) of 0.89 across 23 drugs in 2,021 Shigella sonnei isolates from BV-BRC; geographic and temporal holdouts included.
existing_models.authors_named_unsolved: Resistance not explained by known determinants, drift of resistance over time, scaling to very large datasets.

existing_models.name: AMRFinderPlus known-gene rules (NCBI)
existing_models.score_and_split: No single score; its calls are this dataset's features, so a gene-class rule is the natural baseline.

backbone.name: ESM-2 (protein language model), 35M or 150M checkpoint, run on the reference proteins of the AMRFinderPlus hits

integration.partner_dataset: CARD (Comprehensive Antibiotic Resistance Database) ontology and WHO tuberculosis mutation catalogue
integration.join_key: ARO antibiotic ontology ID / RefSeq protein accession
integration.bigger_question_one_sentence: Which drug-species combinations show resistance that known gene catalogues can't explain, and is that gap growing over time or concentrated in particular regions?

controls.positive_control: Klebsiella carbapenemase genes (KPC/NDM/OXA-48/VIM/IMP) predicting meropenem resistance (verified 85% vs 6% resistant); also beta-lactamase genes predicting ampicillin resistance in E. coli.
controls.negative_control: Shuffle labels within species×drug; drop the gene class matching the drug and confirm the predictive signal collapses.
controls.external_validation: Train on isolates collected up to 2017, test on 2018–2025; and hold out whole countries or source databases (NARMS vs PATRIC).

honest_claim_h3: Among sequenced isolates of WHO priority pathogens that someone tested and deposited publicly (mostly North American, mostly from 2015–2020), presence of known AMRFinderPlus genes and mutations predicts lab-measured resistance with accuracy X per species×drug, and that accuracy falls by Y on unseen countries or later years. This excludes M. tuberculosis, which has no mutation calls here, and cannot detect resistance mechanisms outside the catalogue.

plain_idea.one_liner: Use the list of known resistance genes found in each bacterial genome to predict whether a lab test will show antibiotic resistance.
plain_idea.train_on: For each isolate, a yes/no list of ~2,000 known resistance genes and mutations, paired with each antibiotic tested; about 1.38M labelled isolate–drug rows across 164,609 genotyped isolates.
plain_idea.predict: Resistant versus susceptible to a given antibiotic, as measured in the lab by dilution or disk tests and recorded by the original studies and surveillance databases.
plain_idea.why_worthwhile: Gene-catalogue curators and genome-based diagnostics developers would see exactly which species, drugs, regions and years the catalogue fails for, and therefore where unknown resistance mechanisms are hiding.

label_elsewhere.sources: BV-BRC/PATRIC, NCBI antibiograms, NARMS (the US foodborne resistance surveillance program) and Pathogenwatch all hold lab susceptibility results (known resources, and already merged into CABBAGE); CRyPTIC (an international tuberculosis consortium) holds about 12k tuberculosis isolates with MICs (known, not checked).
label_elsewhere.why: CABBAGE already pools these, so source-held-out validation (e.g. train on PATRIC, test on NARMS) is available inside one file.

pitch.headline: 1.38M lab-measured resistance labels across 164,609 genotyped bacterial isolates, 58 species and 153 countries, in 41 MB of open parquet.
pitch.what_makes_the_data_unusual: Gene and mutation calls come precomputed and keyed on BioSample, so there is no genome processing. Collection year (78% filled) and source database allow temporal and cross-source holdouts; earlier benchmarks used 31,195 PATRIC genomes.
pitch.the_win: A per species×drug map of where the known-gene rule fails on post-2018 or held-out-country isolates, with ML recovering a stated MCC gain over the rule on those cells.
pitch.even_if_it_fails: If ML only matches the gene rule, that is evidence the catalogue already explains resistance for those drugs, and the cells where both fail mark candidate unknown mechanisms.
pitch.who_wants_it: The CABBAGE/Imperial MRC Centre group, NCBI AMRFinderPlus curators and the JRaviLab amR developers deciding which drug-species gaps to curate next.

ml_idea: Pivot the AMRFinderPlus hits into a binary isolate×gene matrix, then fit per species×drug logistic and gradient-boosted models for resistant vs susceptible against a known-gene-class rule. Evaluate on held-out country, held-out source database and a post-2017 temporal split. Optionally add ESM-2 embeddings of hit proteins so unseen alleles can be scored. Exclude M. tuberculosis (no point-mutation calls).

effort.compute_note: Load times observed while inspecting (seconds per file); RAM, ESM-2 time for ~2,177 proteins and cross-validation time on a ~165k × 2k sparse matrix are estimates, not timed.
effort.cheapest_killing_check: For the top 30 species×drug pairs, compute the known-gene rule's balanced accuracy on a post-2017 holdout. If it is already above 0.95 everywhere, little is left for ML, and the project shrinks to a rule-failure note.

verdict_reason: Data verified: clean, large, open, label is a lab-measured column, and a positive control works. But the field is crowded with open models and the known-gene rule may already be near the ceiling; run the rule-baseline check first. M. tuberculosis (331k rows) is unusable without point-mutation calls.
